newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian traders see LME copper firm, directionless.
newsitem.headline: Asian traders see LME copper firm, directionless.

text.p: The direction of copper prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) was impossible to predict for the short-term, traders in Asia said on Monday, but there was no doubt of the red metal's underlying strength.
"Firm but directionless," said a Singapore-based trader.
"There's no major news, no rumours, there's no significant interest on the part of the fundamental users of the market, so I think it will move pretty much sideways," he said.
Declines in LME copper stocks of close to 10,000 tonnes last week saw prices rise on Friday to their highest point in almost a year.

The metal's price hit a new 11-1/2-month high of $2,488 per tonne early in the session, but failed to hold the level. By the end of the session, three months copper was at $2,466 a tonne, just $3 up on Thursday's close.
The high prices will keep Chinese buyers out of the market, traders in Hong Kong and China said.
"Chinese customers just cannont accept these LME levels," said a trader in Hong Kong with a state-owned Chinese firm.
But he saw the threat of drought and subsequent electricity supply problems in Chile, coupled with on-going labour disputes, as helping copper maintain its current strength.
Aluminium was seen range-bound for now, though traders throughout the region said they were optimistic its price would breach $1,700 a tonne in the medium-term.
With the LME the only current source of the metal, the stock drawdowns that have been a feature of aluminium's recent rally were expected to continue, traders said.
In Friday trading on the LME, aluminium tested $1,670 but failed to hold, closing at $1,666.50 a tonne.
Brandeis (Brokers) Limited said in a daily market review that aluminium's upside was limited for now and a test of support at $1,650 may be seen this week.
